title: TCP vs UDP: The Cost of Reliability

sources.title: RFC 9293 — Transmission Control Protocol
sources.notes: Byte-stream service, sequence numbers, SYN/FIN sequence space, three-way handshake, cumulative acknowledgments and receive windows.

sources.title: RFC 768 — User Datagram Protocol
sources.notes: UDP datagram service does not guarantee delivery or duplicate protection.

sources.title: RFC 5681 — TCP Congestion Control
sources.notes: Congestion window and receiver window are distinct constraints on sending.

sources.title: RFC 9000 — QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport
sources.notes: QUIC demonstrates reliable transport capabilities layered over UDP datagrams.

sections.title: Two transports, one unreliable network
sections.narration: TCP or UDP: which one is better? That's like asking whether every task needs the same group-project plan. Let's look at what each service does when data goes missing, and choose based on what the application actually needs.
bullets: IP can lose or reorder packets
sections.takeaway: Choose a transport by the behavior the application needs.

sections.title: Ports identify application endpoints
sections.narration: An IP address gets us to a network endpoint. A port helps identify the application endpoint there. Follow that destination port to the right place. These are numbered endpoints, not tiny physical holes where the packets plug in.
sections.takeaway: Ports help a host deliver incoming transport data to the right endpoint.

sections.title: UDP preserves datagram boundaries
sections.narration: UDP sends separate messages called datagrams. If one arrives intact, the application can still recognize its boundary. But UDP itself doesn't promise that every datagram arrives, arrives in order, or arrives only once. Those are separate requirements.
bullets: No built-in delivery or order guarantee
sections.takeaway: UDP exposes datagrams without TCP’s reliable ordered byte-stream service.

sections.title: TCP exposes a byte stream
sections.narration: TCP gives us an ordered stream of bytes. HEL, LO, and an exclamation mark can become one stream. It doesn't preserve the original write boundaries. The application needs its own way to recognize where a complete message ends.
sections.takeaway: TCP preserves byte order, not the application’s original write boundaries.

sections.title: First establish a connection
sections.narration: Before our TCP exchange, both sides need to agree on starting sequence information. That's what the three-way handshake helps establish. Think shared starting notes for the conversation, rather than reserving a private road across the Internet.
sections.takeaway: The handshake synchronizes both directions of sequence space.

sections.title: Step one: the client sends SYN
sections.narration: The client sends SYN with sequence number one hundred. SYN uses one sequence position, so the first data byte will start at one hundred and one. Even the introduction takes a numbered place in this example.
bullets: First client data will start at 101
sections.takeaway: SYN consumes one sequence number.

sections.title: Step two: SYN plus acknowledgment
sections.narration: The server replies with its own starting sequence, five hundred, and ACK one hundred and one. There are two directions to track. The server's sequence numbers and its acknowledgment of the client aren't the same counter.
bullets: Each direction has its own numbering
sections.takeaway: An acknowledgment names the next sequence position expected.

sections.title: Step three: acknowledge the server
sections.narration: The client returns ACK five hundred and one. Now both sides have the starting state for our connection. The client's next data can begin at one hundred and one. Three messages, and we're ready to continue the conversation.
bullets: ACK alone consumes no sequence number
sections.takeaway: Both endpoints now know the peer’s starting sequence space.

sections.title: Number bytes, not whole packets
sections.narration: Here's the number trick: TCP counts bytes, not packets. One hundred bytes starting at sequence one hundred and one run through two hundred. So a different packet size doesn't change what those byte positions mean.
sections.takeaway: A segment’s sequence number identifies its first data byte.

sections.title: Cumulative acknowledgment
sections.narration: ACK two hundred and one means, 'I've got the earlier bytes; this is what I need next.' It confirms the received run in order. Keep thinking next expected byte, rather than last packet seen on the screen.
sections.takeaway: TCP’s acknowledgment number identifies the next expected byte.

sections.title: Packets arrive out of order
sections.narration: Later bytes arrive before the missing middle. The receiver can store bytes three hundred and one through four hundred, but it still needs two hundred and one next. The cumulative ACK stays there until the gap is filled.
bullets: Later bytes can wait in a buffer
sections.takeaway: Receiving later data does not remove an earlier gap in an ordered stream.

sections.title: Recover the missing byte range
sections.narration: The missing middle range is sent again. Once it arrives, the receiver has everything through byte four hundred in order, so ACK four hundred and one can move forward. One repaired gap unlocks the waiting data behind it.
sections.takeaway: Reliability comes from detecting gaps and retransmitting missing data.

sections.title: A lost acknowledgment is not lost data
sections.narration: What if the data arrived but its ACK disappeared? The sender may repeat the segment. The receiver mustn't deliver those bytes to the application twice. It can confirm the same received data again without copying the stream again.
bullets: Duplicate bytes are not delivered twice
sections.takeaway: Sequence space supports duplicate detection as well as ordering.

sections.title: Reliability adds state and delay
sections.narration: Some later bytes are ready, but the application still has to wait for the missing earlier ones. That's part of ordered delivery. Keeping everything in order needs both buffer space and time to recover the gap.
bullets: An early gap can delay later bytes
sections.takeaway: Reliability is a useful service with resource and timing costs.

sections.title: Protect the receiver with flow control
sections.narration: The receiver tells the sender how much space it has left. Here, two hundred bytes fill part of a three-hundred-byte buffer, leaving one hundred. That's flow control: helping the sender avoid overflowing the receiver's limited storage.
sections.takeaway: Flow control addresses the receiver’s capacity.

sections.title: Watch the receive window change
sections.narration: Fill that last hundred bytes, and the available space reaches zero. Then the application reads two hundred bytes, making room again. The receiver can advertise new space. A full inbox can open up once someone actually reads it.
sections.takeaway: An advertised window can change as the application drains its buffer.

sections.title: Congestion control protects the path
sections.narration: The receiver may have room while a router along the path is overloaded. That's a different problem. Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control responds to the network path. Sending sensibly means paying attention to both limits.
bullets: Receiver capacity differs from path load
sections.takeaway: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network.

sections.title: UDP under the same packet loss
sections.narration: A UDP datagram disappears. UDP itself doesn't automatically send it again, and later datagrams may still arrive. The application decides what to do about the gap: recover it, replace it, or accept that this update is gone.
bullets: Missing datagrams stay missing in UDP
The application decides how to react
sections.takeaway: UDP does not add TCP’s retransmission and ordering behavior.

sections.title: Applications can build above UDP
sections.narration: Using UDP doesn't ban reliability. An application protocol can add ACKs, retries, encryption, and congestion control above it. Those features are coming from that protocol, though. UDP hasn't secretly turned into TCP when nobody was looking.
bullets: QUIC adds a richer transport service
sections.takeaway: A UDP-based protocol can implement capabilities absent from UDP itself.

sections.title: Faster is the wrong universal label
sections.narration: So 'UDP is always faster' is too simple. Actual delay depends on the application, the network, and what happens after a failure. Compare the work each system does, instead of giving one transport a permanent gold medal.
bullets: Less built-in machinery is not a guarantee
sections.takeaway: Transport choice does not create a universal speed ranking.

sections.title: Choose a service for a file transfer
sections.narration: For a complete file, we normally need every byte in order. Fill the gap, then rebuild the file. TCP's stream service helps with that, but the application still needs to handle message boundaries and possible connection failures.
bullets: Security and durable storage are separate
sections.takeaway: TCP reliability is transport delivery, not every application guarantee.

sections.title: Choose a service for timely updates
sections.narration: Some live updates work differently. If a newer position arrives, an older missing position may no longer be useful. That's an application choice. It isn't a promise that UDP always gives the freshest data or the lowest delay.
bullets: Fresh updates may replace stale ones
sections.takeaway: A useful transport matches the meaning and timing of application data.
sections.short_title: Prefer a fresh update when appropriate

sections.title: Connections also need an ending
sections.narration: Closing TCP also needs a little coordination. Each direction can close separately, and FIN uses a sequence position. Follow the ACKs confirming the close. The exact timing can vary; every conversation doesn't end with one identical diagram.
sections.takeaway: Connection release is part of the transport’s state machine.

sections.title: Answer the transport puzzle
sections.narration: Need a reliable ordered byte stream? TCP supplies that service. Need separate datagrams and control over extra behavior? Consider UDP. Start with the application's needs: completeness, order, and useful timing. Then choose the tool that fits the job.
sections.takeaway: Understand the service contract before choosing the transport.
